notes.meaning: God gave Ezekiel a powerful vision through His Spirit and set him down in the middle of a valley. When the prophet looked around, the ground was covered with human bones. Leaving bones unburied was considered a terrible disgrace, showing that the people had suffered utter defeat.

The Lord led Ezekiel all around the valley so he could see the full picture. Ezekiel noticed that the bones were scattered everywhere and were completely dry. This dryness showed that life had left them long ago, removing any natural hope of them ever living again.

The Lord asked Ezekiel whether these dry bones could ever live again. Looking at the bones with human eyes, coming back to life was impossible, so Ezekiel answered wisely. He placed the answer entirely in God's hands, knowing only the Almighty has the power to raise the dead.

God told Ezekiel to prophesy, which means to proclaim His message, directly to the dry bones. Telling lifeless bones to listen to the word of the Lord sounded foolish to human thinking. Yet Ezekiel was called to trust that God's spoken word carries the power to bring life to what is dead.

The Lord announced to the bones that He would put breath into them so they would live. The original word for breath also means wind or spirit. Just as God breathed life into the first man at creation, only He could revive these dead remains.

God promised to rebuild the bodies step by step, adding tendons, muscles, and skin before filling them with breath. When they stood alive, they would recognize that He is the true Lord. God often works through great wonders so His people will know and trust His power.

Ezekiel obeyed and spoke God's message over the valley. As he spoke, a sudden rattling sound broke out, and the ground began to shake. Guided by divine power, each bone moved across the valley and joined perfectly with its matching bone.

As Ezekiel watched, tendons and muscles covered the reconnected skeletons, and skin formed over them. The bodies were now fully built and complete on the outside, but they still lay lifeless. Real life had not yet arrived because there was no breath within them.

The Lord directed Ezekiel to call upon the breath to come from every direction and breathe into these slain bodies. This command was like a prayer asking the Spirit of God to finish the miracle of new life. Preaching God's word had formed the bodies, but calling on God's Spirit was needed to make them alive.

Ezekiel delivered the message as commanded, and breath immediately entered the fallen bodies. They came alive, stood up on their feet, and formed an enormous, powerful army. What had been a hopeless boneyard was now a living force ready for God's service.

God explained the meaning of the vision to Ezekiel. The dry bones represented the entire nation of Israel, who felt completely ruined and forgotten in their exile. They believed their strength had dried up and their hope for the future was totally gone.

God told Ezekiel to comfort the despairing exiles with a wonderful promise. He declared that He would open their graves of captivity and bring them back home to the land of Israel. Although living in exile felt like being buried alive, God had the power to bring them out.

God assured them that they would truly know He is the Lord when He rescued them from captivity. He called them 'My people,' reminding them that their covenant bond with Him was still alive. Experiencing this impossible deliverance would prove God's supreme authority to them.

God promised to place His Holy Spirit within His people so they would truly live, and then settle them securely in their land. This return would be both a spiritual renewal of their hearts and a physical return to their homeland. When this happened, the people would see that God always keeps His word.

The word of the Lord came to Ezekiel with a second message, closely connected to the vision of the dry bones. This new prophecy used an everyday physical object to show how God would heal His divided people.

God instructed Ezekiel to take two wooden sticks and write on each one. On the first stick, he was to write the name of Judah and the tribes joined with the southern kingdom. On the second, he wrote the name of Joseph and Ephraim to represent the northern kingdom that had broken away long ago.

Ezekiel was told to hold the two pieces of wood end to end so they looked like a single stick in his hand. This acted as a living picture for the people watching him. It showed that the painful split between the two kingdoms would finally come to an end.

God told Ezekiel that his countrymen would ask what this demonstration meant. The prophets often performed visual actions to stir up interest and draw out questions. Their curiosity opened the door for Ezekiel to share God's plan of reunion.

Ezekiel had to answer that God Himself would take the two divided kingdoms and join them together in His own hand. Human leaders had torn the tribes apart, but God's strength would reunite them into one nation. Under His care and blessing, they would stand undivided once again.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Latter-day Saints teach that the two sticks represent two sacred books, the Bible (the stick of Judah) and the Book of Mormon (the stick of Joseph), joined together as one scriptural witness.

notes.meaning: Ezekiel was told to keep the inscribed sticks in his hand where everyone could clearly see them as he spoke. This kept the visual lesson right before their eyes. The visible sign reinforced the truth of God's spoken promise.

The Lord promised to gather the scattered Israelites out of all the nations where they had gone and lead them back to their own land. This promise reached beyond the exile in Babylon to include people scattered in every direction. God's faithfulness would bring His wandering people home.

Once back in the land, the people would become a single united nation governed by one king. The old civil war and jealousy that had split them into two kingdoms would never happen again. They would live together on the hills of Israel under one peaceful government.

God promised to cure His people of their attraction to idols and cleanse them from their past rebellions. He would change their hearts so they would no longer turn away into sin. This inner cleansing would restore the covenant relationship where they are His people and He is their God.

God promised that His servant David would rule as king and shepherd over the united flock. Under this leader's care, the people would gladly follow God's commands and walk in His ways. A shepherd-king would guide them into true obedience and peace.

differ.view: King David himself will be raised from the dead to reign as an earthly prince over restored Israel in the future kingdom.
The name David refers to Jesus Christ, the promised descendant of David and Good Shepherd who rules His church forever.

notes.meaning: The people would dwell safely in the land God had given to Jacob, and their children and grandchildren would inherit it forever. Their Davidic leader would remain their prince without end. God's blessings to His covenant family were designed to last through every future generation.

The Lord promised to make an everlasting agreement of peace with His people, blessing their numbers and establishing them in safety. He also promised to place His holy sanctuary among them forever. This meant His presence would remain in their midst and never be taken away again.

God declared that His own dwelling place would be right among His people to watch over and protect them. He would be their God, and they would live as His treasured family. Living in close fellowship with God is the greatest goal of His saving work.

When surrounding nations saw God's holy sanctuary standing permanently among His people, they would recognize who the Lord truly is. They would see that He alone sets His people apart and keeps them holy. God's mercy to Israel would become a witness of His glory to the entire world.
